comparison: Perfect agreement on movement speed control analysis (C69-C72). Both acknowledge the small speed difference and accept the speed-matched analysis as demonstrating that movement cannot fully account for SWR rate differences. Peer review notes this addresses the concern but doesn't fully resolve whether behavioral feedback alone could achieve similar results.

Strong agreement on lack of behavioral effects (C91-C98, C121). Both find no significant memory performance changes attributable to neurofeedback on individual trials. OpenEval and peer reviewers treat this null result as consistent with study design and prior work showing decoupling between replay and trial-by-trial decisions.

Strong agreement on preservation of replay content (C78-C89, C102, C104). Both evaluations affirm that neurofeedback SWRs are comparable to control SWRs in terms of replay fraction, spatial content, behavioral biases, and task-relevance. This is treated as a critical finding showing physiologically relevant ensemble recruitment.

Strong agreement on methodological novelty and significance (C99-C103, C125). Both recognize the technical advance of non-invasive neurofeedback for discrete events in memory task context with preserved replay content. Reviewers unanimously acknowledge this as an exciting new tool extending prior work.

Strong agreement on core neurofeedback efficacy (C37-C38, C53-C55). Both confirm compelling evidence that subjects learned to increase SWR rates during pre-reward period, with approximately 2-fold increases on neurofeedback trials compared to delay trials and controls. All reviewers explicitly affirm this finding.

Agreement on rate modulation mechanism (C47-C48). Both accept that subjects modulated SWR occurrence rate rather than event size to meet neurofeedback criteria. Peer review explicitly notes this as a learned strategy to generate events more efficiently.

Strong agreement on compensatory SWR regulation (C56-C57, C60-C62). Both confirm that increased pre-reward SWRs were followed by decreased post-reward SWRs, resulting in normalized total SWR counts. All reviewers explicitly acknowledge this compensatory finding as evidence of homeostatic regulation.

Agreement on short-timescale homeostatic regulation (C73-C75, C117-C120, C124). Both accept evidence for homeostatic control of SWR production operating over short timescales with multiple regulatory mechanisms. Peer review notes uncertainty about whether this represents neurofeedback-specific versus behavioral feedback effects, which OpenEval does not address.

Agreement on behavioral compensation via dwell time (C64-C65, C68). Both accept that subjects left reward wells earlier on neurofeedback trials, contributing to compensatory reduction in post-reward SWRs. Peer reviewers treat this as part of the homeostatic mechanism without challenge.

Divergence on mechanistic interpretation (C108-C109). OpenEval rates these claims as UNCERTAIN speculation about brain-wide state changes and downstream recruitment. Peer review raises more fundamental uncertainty about whether effects are specifically neural versus behavioral, questioning if behavioral feedback alone could achieve similar results. Peer concern is more critical of the neurofeedback mechanism itself.

OpenEval identifies speculative future applications (C126-C133) as UNCERTAIN, noting claims about disease models, aging, and human translation are untested. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these future application claims.

OpenEval identifies background/context claims (C1-C17, C36, C76) as SUPPORTED well-established knowledge. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these background claims, as peer reviews focus on novel findings.

OpenEval identifies prior work characterization (C19-C35) as SUPPORTED, establishing gaps and distinctions from existing approaches. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these literature review claims.
OpenEval rates prediction about consolidation effects (C123) as UNCERTAIN speculation about future experiments. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses this specific prediction.

OpenEval rates functional interpretations of dysregulated replay (C112-C116) as UNCERTAIN speculation, noting behavioral consequences are untested. No corresponding peer review evaluation explicitly addresses these speculative functional claims.

Partial overlap on learning strategy (C49-C50). Both address that subjects learned to modulate SWR rates efficiently. OpenEval groups this with broader neurofeedback efficacy claims, while peer review focuses specifically on the rate modulation mechanism.

Partial overlap on replay diversity and task-relevance (C105-C107). OpenEval treats these as supporting preserved replay content. Peer review addresses these in context of mechanistic uncertainty about whether neurofeedback recruits physiologically relevant ensembles through neural versus behavioral pathways.
